story.text: The Second World War was over. Vannevar Bush, who had led the scientific communities efforts to support this effort now had time to reimagine, looking now to a new future.

In an article published in the Atlantic, he explore how humans might be able to interact with emergent technology to unlock new possibility for learning. To focus his musings, he created the concept of theoretical new tool that he called a 'memex'. A concept that laid the conceptual framework for what was to emerge with Hypertext and the the World Wide Web.

“Consider a future device … in which an individual stores all his books, records, and communications, and which is mechanized so that it may be consulted with exceeding speed and flexibility. It is an enlarged intimate supplement to his memory.” Vannevar Bush, Atlantic, July 1945."
A paradigm that has unleashed new ways of thinking and the potential for new creativity. A world that now challenges us to reimagine the very experience of education.
Here is how Bush describes in this article the experience of using this theoretical memex:

The owner of the memex, let us say, is interested in the origin and properties of the bow and arrow. Specifically he is studying why the short Turkish bow was apparently superior to the English long bow in the skirmishes of the Crusades. He has dozens of possibly pertinent books and articles in his memex. First he runs through an encyclopedia, finds and interesting but sketchy article, leaves it projected, Next, in a history, he finds another pertinent item, and ties the two together. Thus he goes, building a trail of many items. Occasionally he inserts a comment of his own, either linking it into the main trail or joining it by a side trail to a particular item. When it becomes evident that the elastic properties of available materials had a great deal to do with the bow, he branches off on a side trail which takes him through textbooks on elasticity and tables of physical constants. He inserts a page of longhand analysis of his own. Thus he builds a trail of his interest through the maze of materials available to him

And his trails do not fade. Several years later, his talk with a friend turns to the queer ways in which a people resist innovations, even of vital interest. He has an example, in the fact that the outranged Europeans still failed to adopt the Turkish bow. In fact he has a trail on it. A touch brings up the code book. Tapping a few keys projects the head of the trail. A lever runs through it at will, stopping at interesting items, going off on side excursions. It is an interesting trail, pertinent to the discussion. So he sets a reproducer in action, photographs the whole trail out, and passes it to his friend for insertion in his own memex, there to be linked into the more general trail.
The name "memex" was possibly derived from "memory index". It might also stand for "memory extender".
What Bush describes is remarkably similar to the experience of creating and sharing [[Memory Patterns]] in a fedwiki.
[[The Dayton Experiment]] was originally written in the fedwiki. It contains stories, concepts, and trails that others could easily access later.
An experience that illuminated an understanding of the potential of hypertext - inspired by Borge and Bush - to a new level.
What a relief not to have to keep all of those ideas in one's head anymore. And to know that the trails from this important work will not easily fade, increasing our [[Temporal Thickness]].
